name: Mealie
description: Recipe manager that imports recipes, plans meals, builds shopping lists, and keeps a household cookbook in one web app.

screenshots.caption: Recipe library home screen with search, categories, and saved recipes.
Mobile-friendly recipe view for browsing recipes from a phone.
Home Assistant card integration showing meal plan information.

editorial.get_started:
Most people should start with the official Docker Compose examples. Mealie runs as a web app on port 9000 inside the container, stores app data in a mounted volume, and can use SQLite for smaller households or PostgreSQL for busier installs.

Before adding a real recipe library, choose the database path, set `BASE_URL`, keep signups closed unless you intentionally want open registration, and decide how backups will leave the server. If the data volume lives on a NAS, use PostgreSQL instead of SQLite.
editorial.verdict: Mealie is a strong pick for households that want recipes, meal planning, and shopping lists in one private app. The tradeoff is that the recipe library becomes real personal data, so backups and database choice matter more than they do for a disposable dashboard.
good_fit: Families replacing recipe apps or shared notes
Meal planning and grocery list workflows
Users who want URL recipe imports plus manual recipe entry
watch_outs: Tiny installs where backups are an afterthought
SQLite setups placed directly on NAS storage
People who need polished native mobile apps
known_issues: SQLite is convenient, but PostgreSQL is safer for NAS storage or higher concurrency.
Recipe images, backups, and imports can make the data volume grow over time.
PostgreSQL restores have extra permissions steps compared with SQLite restores.

resources.cpu_notes: Light CPU needs for normal recipe browsing and meal planning. Import jobs, OCR-like parsing, and larger households can add short bursts of work.

data.storage_and_data_notes: Mealie stores recipes, meal plans, shopping lists, users, groups, settings, uploaded images, generated backups, and import-related data. SQLite installs keep the main database and app data under the mounted `/app/data/` path. PostgreSQL installs split state between the Mealie data volume and the Postgres database volume.
data.backup_details:
For SQLite installs, stop the container when practical and back up the full mounted Mealie data folder, then keep copies somewhere outside the host. The built-in backup feature is useful, but it should not be the only copy if the server or disk fails.

For PostgreSQL installs, back up the database and the Mealie data volume together. A restore test should prove that recipes, images, user accounts, meal plans, shopping lists, and login all work on a fresh container. PostgreSQL restores can require temporary elevated database permissions, so document that before an emergency.
data.raid_notes: RAID can help keep a recipe server online if a disk fails, but it is not a backup. For most Mealie installs, versioned offsite backups of the data volume and database matter more. If the app is stored on a NAS, prefer PostgreSQL over SQLite and still keep separate restore-tested backups.

hardware_recommendations.label: Existing Docker host or small VPS
hardware_recommendations.reason: Mealie is usually light enough for the server already running your reverse proxy and household apps, as long as the data volume and backups are planned.
hardware_recommendations.price_note: Use existing hardware first unless recipe images or family usage grow.

hardware_recommendations.label: Mini PC with reliable storage for family use
hardware_recommendations.reason: For a shared household cookbook, prioritize dependable storage, scheduled backups, and PostgreSQL if the data lives near NAS storage.
hardware_recommendations.price_note: A basic mini PC is enough for most households.
